item.title: Is React(tanstack) Query Too Biased? Deep dive: Real Life Data Fetching Practices — Chapter 1
item.description: The hidden gem behind the React query is revealed. Take a gigantic dive into the traditional ways of data fetching vs newfangled ways where the term "query" is mentioned.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome aboard to the very first session!. I'm thrilled to share something with you especially when it's first — always makes the things more valuable(at least for me). I intended to cover **traditional ways of data fetching vs. newfangled ways** in Javascript. I'll try to address the answer of cause-effect relations. In addition, This is one of three chapters(might be more, I'm just saying) under the same name with this article. Well, no more fluffs. Let's dive into the logic. 1. [What is a query?](#what-is-a-query) - [Database Query](#database-query) - [Web Search Query](#web-search-query) - [Query String](#query-string) 2. [What is React Query?](#what-is-react-query) - [Overview](#overview) - [Common usage scenarios](#common-usage-scenarios) 3. [The Big Picture: The Evolution of Data Fetching in JavaScript](#the-big-picture--evolution-of-data-fetching-in-javascript) - [Pre-AJAX Web Experience (1999 and older)](#the-before-ajax-in-other-words-pre-ajax-web-experience-1999-and-older) - [The AJAX Revolution with `XMLHttpRequest` (Early 2000s)](#the-ajax-revolution-with-xmlhttprequest-early-2000s) - [Promises (ES6/ECMAScript 2015)](#promises-es6ecmascript-2015) - [The Fetch API (Around 2015/2016)](#the-fetch-api-around-20152016) - [Async/Await (ES2017)](#asyncawait-es2017) - [Modern Libraries and Frameworks](#modern-libraries-and-frameworks) 4. [Bottom line](#bottom-line) 5. [What next on chapter 2?](#what-next-on-chapter-2) > [id=warning] **Disclaimer:** None of my writing includes direct source of AI. All concrete, synthesized with the original source and my own conclusions/summaries. LLMs are only used to access specific knowledge bases or to create informative diagrams. ## What is a query? To address the related clarification for this article, I suppose that we must go back to the very beginning of the term **"querying"**. In dictioneries such as [oxford dictionary](https://www.oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com/definition/english/query_1), a query _/ˈkwɪəri/_ indicated as anglicized form of the Latin imperative **'quaere!'**, used in the 16th century. In English as a verb in the sense **inquire** and as a noun meaning **‘query’**, from Latin quaerere **‘ask, seek’**. In other words, it is a question or **request for information**. When it comes to computer science, the term has specific — typically posed to a search engine or a database written in a special language, such as **SQL** to retrieve, add, change, or delete data known as _‘CRUD’_ that you might likely familiar with. I believe, every reactive machine _eventually does a CRUD_ and it is the thing that makes it **reactive**. You can think it as a high-level component inside your computer that provides you to read this article or when updating the research results obtained from a trained AI. As you can see, we can expand on examples numerous times — from the most primitive to the most advanced tech-beings where people utilize them, in various and common scenarios. The brain is actually does millions of queries as well and in my opinion, as other things like planes(looking to the birds and it's aerodynamics), we might have ended-up finding the **"query"** term **by evoking the formations around us**. In our case, _wouldn't it be fitting to make associations with our brains since the brain responds to stimuli just like the `HTTP` req-res cycle?_. As we mentioned earlier, the relevant fields for **"query"** regarding to the intention of this article might be grouped under three headings: - **Database Query** - **Web Search Query** - **Query String** ### Database Query Database query is a request to database management system(DBMS) in order to retrive particular data that is saved in the remote accumilator server. The query usually contains bunch of utilities related to what the query was requested for. Say a fav track in your Spotify, an annoying thumbnail video in Netflix inside the movie listing. All these includes a query itself in stages like **pending** or **success**. ![Diagram of DBMS](https://ytpmpkgcjlcdidphswzv.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/banner/database-management-system-diagram.png) ### Web Search Query A user types into a search engine in order to find information on the web. The search engine processes the query using algorithms to provide a list of relevant results. Better to break down the context list in order for better understanding. [Source used down here](https://www.google.com/intl/en_us/search/howsearchworks/how-search-works/ranking-results/#:~:text=Relevance%20of%20content&text=Our%20systems%20look%20for%20quantifiable,results%20are%20relevant%20to%20queries.). - **Query Interpretation:** The search engine first analyzes the query to understand the user's intent. Corrects spelling errors, recognizes synonyms, and considers the context — say the user's location, language, and search history. - **Indexing**: The system doesn't search the live internet; instead, it rapidly scours it's massive, pre-built, giant database of information gathered by **"web crawlers"** or **"spiders"** that constantly explore and categorize web pages. - **Ranking**: Basically, the search engine assesses the indexed pages for relevance and quality in relation to the query. Hundreds of factors are considered, including: - Content relevance - Quality and authority - User experience(This is where we will deep dive in this article) - Freshness - **Results Presentation:** _The search engine results page_ [(SERP)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Search_engine_results_page) is generated and delivered to the user's browser, typically listing the most relevant results at the top, along with paid advertisements or other features like featured snippets or knowledge panels. > [id=info] When it comes to _SEO_, **the importance of indexing is huge**. Your boring clients most likely wants to see the product in higher-ranks rather than interesting in with the clean-codebase. At this point, [GSC(Google Search Console)](https://search.google.com/) is vital. In order to utilize from the ranking benefits, do not forget to register the app into [GSC(Google Search Console)](https://search.google.com/) for better indexing. In addition, creating meta tags, sitemaps, considering page's render method(SSR, PPR, SSG, CSR) regarding to app's intention are vital as well. FYI: [Search central](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide) ![Serp illustration 1. Credit goes to sitechecker.pro](https://ytpmpkgcjlcdidphswzv.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/banner/serp-illustration.webp) All of these above contribute to **SEO** directly. I couldn't move on without mentioning these things especially when it comes to **query**. ### Query String [Query String](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Query_string) is an optional part of a [URL (Uniform Resource Locator)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/URL) that assigns values to specified parameters, often used to track information or control page appearance. I have noticed that the most common use of a **query string** is to use URL as a shareble/public state managers in the fast-paced evolving modern web. This is what exactly [the twelve factor app](https://12factor.net/processes) indirectly emphasizes. _Using states, which means saving an instance in the client's memory, indeed violates scalability_. When a registered user adds an item to the their shopping cart in the device A(say PC) he should be able to see that added item also in device B(say mobile device). This both creates an impression and _keeping the retention stable that is likely increase purchase rate_. So at the end of the day focusing on being stateless is vital in terms of scalability and accessibility. ![stateless always grater than states](https://ytpmpkgcjlcdidphswzv.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/banner/stateless-greater-than-states.png) As we mentioned earlier, understanding the parts of a URL is **essential knowledge** and **non-trivial fact**. Therefore, I genuinely believe a URL is a must-known thing when it comes to programming and that's why I wanted to cover this topic thoroughly — especially when we're addressing the actual matter of **query**. Down below, I've tried to emphasize decomposition of the URL parts roughly. ![decomposition of a typicial URL](https://ytpmpkgcjlcdidphswzv.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/banner/url-parts-decomposition.png) > [id=info] Interestingly, according to [Tim Berners-Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Berners-Lee) later said the double slashes **'//'** inside a URL were actually unnecessary - they were included based on pre-existing conventions for server names, but he felt they could have been omitted XDD. ## What is React Query? Well, I think we are quite sure about what the **query** is so let's move on our actual topic — **React Query** or we also cane say **Tanstack Query** since the all ecosystem cumulated under one name, which is the great _Tanstack_. ### Overview As the name implies, in my words **React Query is a filling the missing gaps of data-fetching** as mentioned in the official [documentation of Tanstack Query](https://tanstack.com/query/v5/docs/framework/react/overview). Overall, React Query makes fetching, caching, synchronizing and updating server state in web apps. The documentation also emphasizes the common state management libraries, such as redux are not as good as Tanstack _when it comes to server state_ because, their structure designed for genereal use rather than server-driven goods. In this chapter, unlike getting into the weeds of **react query** technical details, it's better to mention it with introduction-like style superficially. Below, I have broken down the subheadings into a list. - Common usage scenarios - Comparison in table view with relevant techs - React Query with React Native ### Common usage scenarios **The main goal of React Query is to serve as a request reducer in any type of web application.** By interacting with network boundaries.
Hot take: When you might not need React Query? It's worth to mentioned that this statement is a **brutal dependent following to your application needings.** If you're building some app that is going to be placed mostly on client-side with client logic like visual editor apps, **then you might not need react query**. Let me introduce you to Dominik, who has already covered the topic and got ideas from people(he will have more information) that built their apps using **React Query**. He is **one of the most valuable maintainer** who played an important role in the development of Tanstack and once he said: > [id=success] _The answer is: You probably don't. If you're starting a new application, and you're using a mature framework like Next.js or Remix that has a good story around data fetching and mutations, you probably don't need React Query. — Ref: [Dominik Dorfmeister](https://tkdodo.eu/blog/you-might-not-need-react-query)_ I agree to disagree with the statement that Dominik said. The reason of disagreement is actually comes from effects in React ecosystem — assuming a client component in client-side **where async logic is not being used**. Take a look at this example: ```tsx import getSession from "./api"; import { useEffect, useState } from "react"; export default function Session({ id }: { id: number }) { const [bio, setBio] = useState(null); useEffect(() => { let ignore = false; setBio(null); getSession(id).then((res) => { if (!ignore) setBio(res); }); return () => { ignore = true; }; }, [id]); return {bio ?? "loading..."}; } ``` The component mounts and _re-renders are prevented in strict mode_ with the `ignore` assignment. This is the traditional way to render `jsx` based on the fetched value. As you may have noticed, I haven't used error handling or an explicit loading statement when fetching data passed from the component prop. Using altogether logic inside `useEffect()` would have made the component unreadable as hell. You can visit a well-written article by Robin, which will provide you a clear conclusion of _hooks and data fetching_ [here](https://www.robinwieruch.de/react-hooks-fetch-data/) That is the point where **React Query** shines. With the single hook provided by `useQuery()`, we can optimize the code in a more predictable, shorter and less tangled way: ```tsx import getSession from "./api"; import { useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query"; export default function Session({ id }: { id: number }) { const { data } = useQuery(["session", id], () => getSession(id), { retry: false, enabled: id !== undefined && id !== null, }); return {data ?? "loading..."}; } ``` > related and written way more comprehensively about React Query [to see the actual big picture](https://tkdodo.eu/blog/). Anyway, let's get back to what he said: > [id=success] Dominik Toretto covering this topic very well, you should definitely check out his [meticulously written articles](https://tkdodo.eu/blog/why-you-want-react-query). Furthermore, this is not just my recommendation — in order to reduce the amount of `useState` in your react app and mitigate the client side bundle work is a non-trivial, inevitable fact: > [id=info] _Consider using or building a client-side cache. Popular open source solutions include TanStack Query(React Query), useSWR, and React Router 6.4+. You can build your own solution too, in which case you would use Effects under the hood but also add logic for deduplicating requests, caching responses, and avoiding network waterfalls (by preloading data or hoisting data requirements to routes) — [Official React Docs](https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect#fetching-data-with-effects)_
Here are some of the most common usage scenarios of React Query: - **Fetching and caching** A paginated product list for an e-commerce category with background refetch to keep prices and availability fresh. - Infinite scroll for a social feed that **loads and caches** additional pages as the user scrolls. - **Prefetching** product details on hover so the detail page opens instantly. - Performing optimistic updates when a user likes a post or edits a comment so the UI updates immediately while the **mutation** runs. - Sharing a **cached** authenticated user profile across header, settings, and dashboard components **to avoid duplicate network requests**. As you may noticed, fetching, prefetching, mutating, caching and so on. Simply put, these are all fundamental things when it comes to **data manipulation** directly _correlated with UX, DX, UI_. It makes life easier for developers by eliminating the need to rewrite everything from scratch. Speaking of which, let's take a quick look like a speed run in minecraft at data fetching in chronological order. --- ## The big picture — evolution of data fetching in Javascript Moving on without addressing this topic would have left people wondering. We have mentioned just the latest modern data fetching methods until now. So for the sake of this article, I have also decided to mention the evolution of data fetching in Javascript with quick snippets to fill all the missing gaps. Grouped everything for you in chronological order for better impact. ### The **'Before AJAX'** in other words, pre-AJAX Web Experience (1999 and older) Before AJAX, the traditional web model was **synchronous** and **page-driven**, meaning virtually every user interaction that required new data from a server resulted in a full page and of course with a rigid pattern. Imagine praying just to not see a white screen. How boring... ![pre-ajax web experience cycle](https://ytpmpkgcjlcdidphswzv.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/banner/pre-ajax-web-experience-cycle.webp) This model followed a rigid pattern: 1. **User Interaction:** User would click a link or submit an HTML form using a `GET` or `POST` request. 2. **Browser Request:** The user's **screen would often go blank(see image below)** or show a loading indicator as it waited for the response. 3. **Server Processing:** When retrieved the necessary data, and dynamically **generated an entire new HTML page** (or updated a full page template). 4. **Full Page Reload:** The server sent the complete HTML response back to the browser. The browser then **discarded the current page entirely** and rendered the new one from scratch, along with all associated assets like images, CSS, and JavaScript files. ![During second step on request the user's screen be like](https://ytpmpkgcjlcdidphswzv.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/banner/flashbang-csgo.webp) ### The AJAX Revolution with `XMLHttpRequest` (Early 2000s) The introduction of async JavaScript and _XML (AJAX) was groundbreaking_. When came out it was pretty promising no more clunky experience for users in early 2000s and the sector had practically revived as it made background jobs possible after named **payload**. Long live `XMLHttpRequest`! **Mechanism:** XHR or in long from `XMLHttpRequest` uses event handlers and callbacks to manage the different stages of a request and eventually returns an observable object. **Limitations:** This approach was verbose and could lead to one of first-seen **"callback hell"** problems in js history with deeply nested callbacks for multiple requests, _making code difficult to read, manage, and debug._ A `XMLHttpRequest` example can be given like down below: ```ts const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest(); xhr.open("GET", "https://burakdev.com/sitemap.xml", true); xhr.responseType = "xml"; xhr.onload = () => { if (xhr.status >= 200 && xhr.status < 300) { console.log("data:", xhr.response); } else { console.error("error:", xhr.status); } }; xhr.onerror = () => { console.error("network error"); }; xhr.send(); ``` > [id=error] **Caveats:** Please pardon for my ignorance, but I've realized something that you might say _"Oh Burak seriously?"_. Node.js doesn't have `XMLHttpRequest` built into its runtime — it never did. When trying to execute what I have written above in my node(v24.0.1) snippet. But instead, I've encountered this error and wanted to mention: ```bash const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest(); ^ ReferenceError: XMLHttpRequest is not defined. ``` #### Current use cases of `XMLHttpRequest` 1. **Progress tracking for file uploads** XHR or with long form `XMLHttpRequest` has **better native support** for monitoring the progress of file uploads than the Fetch API. For this reason, some devs still use XHR specifically for this task. 2. **Support for older browsers** Supported by older browsers that **lack the Fetch API**. While the need for this is diminishing, it can be relevant in certain niche scenarios or for certain user bases. Acting like a **polyfill/fall**. 3. **Setting headers** [View more about the implementation](https://www.greatfrontend.com/pt-BR/questions/quiz/what-are-the-differences-between-xmlhttprequest-and-fetch) Bottom line with XHR, sticking to modern solutions like the built-in `fetch()` method that we're about to talk about yields the best results when it comes to data fetching. ### Promises (ES6/ECMAScript 2015) As I mentioned above, the _callback problems had gone off the rails with XHR_. This created an opportunity for the core maintainers of the modern web to invent at least one workaround that would turn into a specification. Then, in ES6, JavaScript officially introduced Promises as an emergent feature. Unlike nested callbacks — developers now could chain `.then()` methods for successful responses and a `.catch()` method for error handling, resulting in flatter and more readable code. _A tiny spoiler from one of the next heading: once standard `async/await` was introduced, the developer's life became easier and hence, because of its's alignment with promises._
Deep dive: Execution order in ES6 when working with promises Wanted to emphasize one crucial point that you might have missed. Promises and the event loop execution order differs and matters when it comes to [v8 engine](https://v8.dev/) > [id=info] _V8 is Google’s open source high-performance JavaScript and WebAssembly engine, written in C++. It is used in Chrome and in Node.js, among others, implements ECMAScript and WebAssembly and runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux systems that use x64, IA-32, or ARM processors. V8 can be embedded into any C++ application._ Take a look at this snippet and try to guess the execution order: ```ts // phase 1 const req = new Promise((res) => { setTimeout(() => console.log("a"), 2000); console.log("b"); }); req.then((res) => { console.log(res); console.log("c"); }); ``` Then, validate your guess with the snippet below: --- The logged result for the _phase 1_ yields: ```ts // b <-- first instant // a <-- second — after 2 sec ``` Do not get me wrong, don't wanna be brain-rotted, hype-seeker and toxic linkedin user that appears randomly in the shuffle who mostly shares content kinda like "x = 1; y = 2; so z=?..". Thanks to linkedin's algorithm that perfectly matches with user's interesting... I mention these basics, it's just because of the relativity with the topic we currently addressing. Coming back to the _phase 1_, **why the result did not yield also 'c'?**. Where the hell 'c' vanished? Well, it's just **because the promise never resolved.** The promise remains in **pending state** because `res()` is never called. So let's implement it as well: ```ts // phase 2 const req = new Promise((res) => { setTimeout(() => console.log("a"), 2000); res("b"); }); req.then((res) => { console.log(res); console.log("c"); }); // b <-- first instant // c <-- second instant // a <-- third — after 2 sec ``` Now, look's like we're getting the results as we expected. If we put them in **execution order**: 1. **Synced execution**: added to call stack - `setTimeout`, registered as a _macrotask_ - `res('b')`, resolved and called immediately 2. **Microtask queue** - `then()` callback is added to the _microtask queue_ - Microtasks execute _before_ any macrotasks - Prints `b` then `c` 3. Macrotask queue - `setTimeout` callback executes - Prints `a` So, take another guess now. What if we call the `resolve` inside `setTimeout` like shown below? Will it be `a` or `b`: ```ts // phase 3 const req = new Promise((res) => { setTimeout(() => { console.log("a"); res("b"); }, 2000); }); req.then((res) => { console.log(res); console.log("c"); }); ``` Now things changes a bit naturally since have we used the resolver inside the timeout. Corresponding answer for the _phase 3_ is half tricky due to the logic itself. It yields alphabetically but..: ```ts // a <-- after 2 sec // b <-- after 2 sec // c <-- after 2 sec right after 'b' ``` Oh Javascript lovely javascript... In this case things gets bigger Capitan. Understanding the fundamentals of event loop in javascript is actually requires a pure focus — so I recommend you to bring a cup of coffee as we dig more to stay focused ☕ Take a look this illustration to picture holy-canvas: ![javascript event loop](https://ytpmpkgcjlcdidphswzv.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/banner/js-event-loop.gif) [Also check out Lydia's meticulous article covering event loops and task queues in much greater detail than I did.](https://www.lydiahallie.com/blog/event-loop) Then come back please, I do not want to just giveaway my audience 😊 Coming back to the problem, `res('b')` added to an assigned macro-queue and JS talks with the v8: > [id=success] _Hey man stop! Take it easy for a while... Remember, we can only handle one thing at a time!_ Therefore, the **execution order** differs like this: 1. **Synced execution — (immediate)** - `setTimeout`, registered as a _macrotask_ but for 2(s) later - Promise remains in **pending state** (no immediate resolution) - `then()` callback is registered but won't execute yet (waiting an order from v8 for resolving the promise) 2. **Macrotask executes after 2 seconds** - `console.log('a')` executes and prints `a` - `res('b')` is called, resolving the promise with value `b` - This adds the `then()` callback to the **microtask queue!!** 3. Microtask queue (immediately after macrotask): - `then()` callback executes - Prints `b` then `c` **Key takeaway** would be _any changes to micro and macro tasks always matter_. And as a reminder, It's worth to mention that we're still in 2015 with lack of `async/await`. **Synced > Microtasks > Macrotasks** has been the rule since _promises_ were introduced in ES2015. ![javascript event loop priorization](https://ytpmpkgcjlcdidphswzv.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/banner/synced-microtask-macrotask.png) The next few articles for better clarification, I'm planning to cover low-level and lexical addressing in more detail highlighting the **event loops in interpreters**. _Phase 3_ also raises new questions like, what if we relocate the order of `console.log('a')` that comes first and `res('b')` comes right after? Can you predict the outcome for the following snippet: ```ts // phase 4 const req = new Promise((res) => { setTimeout(() => { res("b"); console.log("a"); }, 2000); }); req.then((res) => { console.log(res); console.log("c"); }); ``` The _phase 4_ yields to: ``` // a <-- after 2 sec // b <-- after 2 sec // c <-- after 2 sec right after 'b' ``` Even though we relocated the position of the internal logic we encountered the same result with the _phase 3_. Unlike the _phase 3_, `console.log('a')` runs before the `then()` handler, not after, because the `console.log('a')` is **part of the synchronous code** inside the setTimeout callback, while the `then()` handler is queued as a microtask that runs after the current task finishes. _The last phase_ included one more variant as `console.log(d)` to see how it unfolded: ```ts // phase 5 const req = new Promise((res) => { console.log("a"); setTimeout(() => { res("b"); }, 2000); }); req.then((res) => { console.log(res); console.log("c"); }); console.log("d"); ``` Yields: ```ts // a // d // (wait 2 seconds) // b // c ``` But what was the underlying reason behind the very first logger `console.log('a')` that is printed first despite the `Promise()` fact? It's because the code in Promise constructor runs **synchronously** when the promise is created, **not when it resolves**. So the promise — when registered, **synced-threatened** the inner logics and remember the picture I shared above about the order that is prioritized with the **synchronous ones first**. And finally, since Javascript is interpreted into byte code that is read from top to bottom, the result is yielded at first with `a` then `d`. The snippet looks tricky, and it is actually. Therefore, **understanding the fundamentals of JavaScript execution order is essential yet challenging.**
### The Fetch API (Around 2015/2016) I guess this one is the most efficient way to get some data from the internet that is being used even in last quarter of 2025. Yet interestingly, it has been 10 years since the built-in `fetch()` method came out as a solution for the refinement of legacy data fetching molds such as `XMLHttpRequest` that we mentioned earlier. Simply put, the `XMLHttpRequest` API was largely superseded by the more modern and efficient **Fetch API, which is built on promises from the ground up**. Thus, `fetch` function started to provide a _simpler, cleaner interface for making network requests_ that led to **better DX** thereby. > [id=success] The eventual breakage was **it's modular design and data streams** that are being used under the hood, which is **beneficial for performance and memory** usage when dealing with large files. Mechanism of the `fetch()` API returns a promise that resolves to a `Response` object. To access the actual returned data, a second promise-based method like `json()` must be called. For better clarification, I've prepared a specific snippet, assuming that our goal is fetching this article's `` tag to prove how up to date and fresh my articles are ✨: ```ts fetch("https://burakdev.com/sitemap.xml", { method: "GET", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/xml" }, }) .then((response) => res.text()) .then((result) => console.log(result) .catch((err) => console.log(err)); ``` This snippet yields: ```ts https://burakdev.com Sat, 15 Nov 2025 00:03:20 GMT yearly 1 https://burakdev.com/blogs Sat, 15 Nov 2025 00:03:20 GMT weekly 0.8 https://burakdev.com/blogs/is-react-tanstack-query-too-biased-deep-dive-real-life-data-fetching-practices-chapter-1 Fri, 14 Nov 2025 23:11:58 GMT yearly 0.5 ``` And yeah, I slightly realized the date format I used inside `` tag is not following the [W3 ISO STANDART](https://www.w3.org/TR/NOTE-datetime). While I get to work on this, you may have a look this [microsoft report](https://blogs.bing.com/webmaster/february-2023/The-Importance-of-Setting-the-lastmod-Tag-in-Your-Sitemap) about sitemaps where we mentioned the importance of sitemaps right above in [Web search query](#what-is-a-query) section. > [id=info] **58% of hosts have at least one XML sitemap** (sitemap known by Bing) while **42% of hosts don’t have one XML sitemap (Bing does not know it)**, this is absolutely insane! Almost half of the web, opt-out from indexing boundaries by crawlers. For those where `` attribute set that is taking the compounds around %84 of sitemaps, %18 have lastmod values not correctly set. — [direct source: Microsoft bing blogs](https://blogs.bing.com/webmaster/february-2023/The-Importance-of-Setting-the-lastmod-Tag-in-Your-Sitemap) I genuinely believe if you haven't grabbed your sitemap yet, _go compose your sitemap ASAP_ in order to use your map because I want you to never forget, _in my articles you're a Capitan and not knowing which way to go is no different from an elderly man walking down a dark, unsafe street without a flashlight being mugged by thieves._ Anyway coming back to `fetch()`. The way I went through right up in the snippet was deliberately uncommon as we used xml with `.text()` method since _the Fetch API does not natively parse XML_. While native fetch can handle most tasks, _Axios provides features that improve the developer experience_ for complex applications. **Interceptors** Allows us to globally intercept and modify requests or responses, which is **useful for adding authentication tokens or logging**. Below I've curated a boilerplate, an instance of auth implementation with axios although I don't love them and one bonus, HTTP authentication diagram.
**Under the macroscope:** HTTP background process while auth with axios interceptors, visualized. > [id=info] Axios, automatically converts JSON data into a JS object, unlike `fetch` as we mentioned in this article. ```ts import axios, { AxiosInstance, InternalAxiosRequestConfig, AxiosResponse, AxiosError, } from "axios"; // A custom Axios instance const apiClient: AxiosInstance = axios.create({ baseURL: "https://api-staff.com/", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", // or whatever the requested content type is and to learn // target-agnostic content type, you can always run // console.log(fetch(URL_TO_FETCH).then((val) => val)); // (without parsing!) // this will return an object containing bunch of // useful information about the identity // of the targetted utility. }, }); const getAuthToken = (): string | null => { // next line not reflects the real-life practices // just arbitary usage — do not try at home return localStorage.getItem("authToken"); }; // This is the request interceptor apiClient.interceptors.request.use( (config: InternalAxiosRequestConfig) => { const token = getAuthToken(); if (token) { config.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`; } return config; }, (error: AxiosError) => { // Handle request errors return Promise.reject(error); } ); // And finally the response interceptor for logging and global error handling apiClient.interceptors.response.use( (response: AxiosResponse) => response, (error: AxiosError) => { console.error(`❌ [API] Error: ${error.message}`); if (error.response && error.response.status === 401) { console.log("Unauthorized request"); } return Promise.reject(error); } ); export default apiClient; ``` For detailed information about authentication and authorization with HTTP, [you can check out the MDN docs](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Authentication). The name comes from an **HTTP cache invalidation strategy** — first returns cached data instantly, then re-fetches the latest data in the background, _thus completing stale—revalidate cycle_ and providing a stream of updates to the UI. - **Simple API:** Provides a very minimal and easy-to-use useSWR hook. - **Automatic Revalidation:** _Automatically re-fetches data_ when the user regains network connection or switches browser tabs. - **Lightweight:** It is a smaller alternative to **React Query**, ideal for simpler data fetching needs. **(The sources say so, NOT me)** #### React Server Components (RSCs) This is the topic I genuinely want to cover in a new episode. RSCs are a relatively _new paradigm that allows developers to run React components exclusively on the server_. Designed to combine the benefits of server-side rendering with the component-based model of React.
